posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md: I was wondering if anyone has tried these for object lighting. They seem to offer two important benefits: more efficient use of light due to the limited divergence of the diffused beam, and some kind of polarization retention. I was reading on the Edmund Optics FAQ (which is quite useful by the way) that holographic diffusers "retard" polarization, but they didn't say how exactly. If it acted like a half-wave plate, that would be good. Even if it acted like a quarter-wave plate, I suppose one could insert another quarter-wave plate in front, so that both optics together would behave as a half-wave plate. Although these Edmund diffusers are expensive, each plastic optic could easily be cut into a multitude of smaller ones.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
I've used holograms of diffusers to make stereograms and for object lighting a few times. They were always homemade on silver halide material, so were polarization preserving. 

Really helps for prevention of stray light going all over the place as with a normal diffuser. The downside is that they are generally custom made for a particular set-up, and really need to have high DE to not waste too much of that expensive laser light.

posts.author: John Klayer
posts.content_md: The price of holographic diffusers kept me from trying them. What I'm using now is a concave diffuse reflector made from the bottom of an aluminum can with a hole in the middle for the beam to enter from the back side with a piece of opal glass at the sort of focus. Some of the light scatters forward as usual, what bounces off the opal glass get reflected forward by the can reflector.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Here is the information on the Edmund holographic diffusers:

[http://www.edmundoptics.com/onlinecatal ... uctid=1363](http://www.edmundoptics.com/onlinecatalog/DisplayProduct.cfm?productid=1363) 

I would really like to test one of these. My main questions are: Does it produce a clean (smooth and uniform) diffusion? If it diffuses an undiverged laser beam, is there a "hot spot" in the center due to the gaussian beam profile? and How does it affect polarization?

These must be successful products, the new Edmund catalog seems to show a vastly expanded number of them, with many different types of diffusing angles. They have "sheet" diffusers which are 2 X 2 inches (0.76mm thick) polycarbonate for $115 each. They offer 13 different diffusing angles for these, 9 of them from 0.5 degree to 80 degrees, and 4 different elliptical angles.

The problem is the cost, and the need to have a selection on hand for different lighting situations. Maybe four of us can get together, and buy one of the 2 X 2 diffusers for testing. I could buy one, cut it into four pieces (1 X 1), and divide them amongst us. Assuming this works out, we could continue this process with additional diffusers with other angles, so that we can build up a collection. If they are $115 each, maybe I could offer the one-inch square pieces to other people for $35 each.

As to the cutting method, since they are polycarbonate, maybe I could use the "hot wire" method (like what they use for cutting styrofoam). I've used this technique to cut some plastic half-wave plates into smaller pieces. This would not involve contacting the central areas of the filters, which could cause damage. (The edge itself might be a bit ragged, but this wouldn't have any affect on performance. Cutting by the "score and snap" method might damage them.)

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
Those diffusers are from Physical Optics Corporation (actually the spin-off company). I use them all the time. They are also referred to as "light shaping diffusers" and are made by a holographic method. The hologram diffusers I mentioned above are actually holograms *of* diffusers.

The POC diffusers' directional and/or shaped lobe of diffusion makes them more efficient than ground glass or other wide lobe diffusers in a hologram recording system. Their "high" cost will probably be waaaay lower than the cost of the photons they save, but only in a studio that's actually making holograms.

posts.content_md: We've all been on the hunt for the perfect diffuser, and have all found household items that work very well. Scotch tape works well too. Most holographers have much bigger issues to face than those presented by use of diffusers found around the home. Myself included. posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
> **Joe:** I was reading on the Edmund Optics FAQ (which is quite useful by the way) that holographic diffusers "retard" polarization, but they didn't say how exactly. If it acted like a half-wave plate, that would be good. Even if it acted like a quarter-wave plate, I suppose one could insert another quarter-wave plate in front, so that both optics together would behave as a half-wave plate.

By retard they mean that it makes a 1/n plate and the value for n is likely to be anything between 2 and 4 depending on the wavelength, angle and optic. What this means to us is your linear polarization is going to be eliptical by a certain degree and you won't know how much till you measure it. 

I guess you could rotate it in front of a polarizer to learn just how eliptical it is. It might be usefull for lowering the glare from a highlight to rotate the holographic diffuser, I have not tried. It works well with 1/2 wave plates.

Just a side note on specular reflections, Bright reflections on a H1 or H2 near the film plane overload the abilities of the film and cause "burn in". You can deal with them by adding a 1/2 wave plate to the object beam and rotating the polarization of the specular reflections so it does not form fringes as well or move the image plane front or backwards to get the reflection out of the film plane. I find even 1/8" can make a difference. (We have talked about this a lot. If anyone wants to learn more search for burn in.)
